blogs.title: When “Shall” Meets Standing: D.C. Circuit Says You Can’t Force OSC to Investigate FOIA Withholdings
blogs.description: The court held that America First Legal Foundation lacked Article III standing to compel the Office of Special Counsel to investigate alleged arbitrary FOIA withholdings under 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3). This post unpacks the court’s causation and redressability analysis, emphasizing the speculative chain of events needed to link an OSC investigation to DOJ’s production of records and the barrier posed by agency enforcement discretion (Heckler v. Chaney). It situates the ruling within the broader trend tightening procedural-injury standing and explains why the injury from non-disclosure is traceable to DOJ—not OSC.

blogs.title: Informational Standing Without an Entitlement: Why § 1216 Doesn’t Grant Access to OSC Investigation Outputs
blogs.description: AFL argued informational injury based on not receiving notices and updates that would accompany an OSC investigation. The D.C. Circuit rejected that theory because § 1216 creates no entitlement to receive information, and the § 1214 notice regime is discretionary in § 1216 investigations (see Carson v. OSC). This post contrasts the court’s approach with Akins and Public Citizen, where Congress expressly created information-access rights, and offers practical takeaways for watchdog groups seeking to premise standing on informational injuries.

blogs.title: The FOIA–OSC Two-Track Enforcement Puzzle the D.C. Circuit Didn’t Decide
blogs.description: The district court held that OSC’s duty to investigate under § 1216(a)(3) is not limited by FOIA’s separate disciplinary-referral trigger in § 552(a)(4)(F), but the D.C. Circuit avoided the merits on standing grounds. This post explores the unresolved statutory-structure question: how § 1216’s general investigative mandate interacts with FOIA’s specific, court-triggered disciplinary scheme. It analyzes potential readings of the two provisions, implications for OSC’s role in FOIA enforcement, and what kinds of future plaintiffs (or fact patterns) might put the merits squarely before the court.

blogs.title: Independent Actors and the Standing Trap: Lessons from AFL v. Greer for Multi-Agency Litigation
blogs.description: Relying on recent Supreme Court guidance, the court rejected a causal chain that depended on multiple independent actors—OSC’s enforcement decisions, MSPB sanctions, and DOJ’s production choices. This post examines the opinion’s use of cases like Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine and Haaland v. Brackeen to tighten redressability when third-party choices control outcomes. It offers strategic guidance for litigants: target the withholding agency directly under FOIA; avoid suits that hinge on persuading separate enforcers; and recognize the limits of using mandatory-investigation language to overcome Article III hurdles.
